content: Tinea nigra, also referred to as superficial phaeohyphomycosis or Tinea nigra palmaris et plantaris, is a superficial fungal infection that manifests as dark brown to black, painless patches on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. These patches are typically asymptomatic and do not cause discomfort. The infection is caused by a fungus that was previously classified as Exophiala werneckii but is now recognized as Hortaea werneckii. In some cases, the causative organism has also been described as Phaeoannellomyces werneckii. The diagnosis of tinea nigra is confirmed through microscopic examination of skin scrapings. These scrapings are treated with potassium hydroxide (KOH), which dissolves non-fungal debris, allowing for the visualization of fungal elements under the microscope. During a physical examination, the characteristic skin findings of tinea nigra are observed. These findings are well-documented in dermatological atlases and are essential for clinical recognition of the condition. Tinea nigra must be distinguished from other dermatological conditions that present with erythematous, scaly, annular, and pruritic rashes. Differential diagnoses include other fungal infections and skin disorders with similar clinical presentations. Treatment for tinea nigra involves the topical application of selenium sulfide-containing dandruff shampoos to the affected areas. Additionally, topical antifungal agents, such as imidazoles like ketoconazole, may be used. This treatment approach is similar to that used for other superficial fungal infections, such as tinea versicolor or pityriasis versicolor.
